title: Functional/Dissociative Seizures (FDS): Neurobiological, Emotional, and Stress-Related Factors and Approaches to Optimizing Care
summary:
Functional or dissociative seizures (FDS) often look very similar to epileptic seizures but are not caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Many affected individuals initially receive an incorrect diagnosis or are not properly diagnosed for years. This frequently leads to burdensome treatment pathways, unnecessary medications, and considerable uncertainty.
Current evidence suggests that FDS may arise from a complex interaction of psychological stress, traumatic experiences, difficulties in emotion regulation, and biological factors. However, it is still not sufficiently understood why some people develop these seizures while others do not. It also remains unclear which factors influence the long-term course of the condition and which treatment approaches are most helpful.
The aim of this study is therefore to comprehensively assess individuals with FDS and compare them with patients who have epilepsy. The study will examine psychological stress, physical comorbidities, everyday stressors, imaging findings, and specific retinal measurements (Optical Coherence Tomography, OCT). In addition, participants may voluntarily use a smartphone app to document aspects of their daily lives in order to better understand possible triggers or early warning signs of seizures.
In the long term, the study aims to improve diagnostic procedures, better identify different subtypes of the condition, and contribute to the development of more targeted treatment approaches. The overall goal is to provide faster, clearer, and more individually tailored care for affected individuals.

interventions.name: Participation in quantitative and qualitative structured interviews, psychometric assessments, smartphone-based assessments as well as analysis of available clinical findings (cMRI, EEG, laboratory, cerebrospinal fluid, and OCT data) as single cross-sectional assessment with the option of longitudin

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Capacity to provide informed consent
Confirmed or suspected diagnosis of functional/dissociative seizures (FDS) or confirmed diagnosis of epilepsy
Sufficient proficiency in the German language
Exclusion criteria:
Acute florid psychosis
Severe cognitive impairment
Lack of capacity to provide informed consent
Severe neurological disorders with substantial diagnostic uncertainty
Acute substance intoxication or manifest substance dependence
Medically unstable patients
